claim: Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses (NCLs) occur in an estimated 2 to 4 of 100,000 live births.
source: The neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses (NCLs) are a class of individually rare, primarily autosomal recessive, neurodegenerative diseases occurring in an estimated 2 to 4 of 100,000 live births (Nita et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nita et al., 2016, which provides the epidemiological data.

claim: NCLs represent the most prevalent class of hereditary pediatric neurodegenerative disease.
source: Collectively, NCLs represent the most prevalent class of hereditary pediatric neurodegenerative disease (Haltia, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Haltia, 2006.

claim: The cardinal feature of all NCLs is the intracellular accumulation of proteolipid material, termed lipofuscin.
source: The cardinal feature of all NCLs is the intracellular accumulation of proteolipid material, termed lipofuscin (Jalanko and Braulke, 2009; Nita et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jalanko and Braulke, 2009 and Nita et al., 2016.

claim: Lipofuscin accumulates most robustly in neurons of affected individuals.
source: While lipofuscin accumulates in all cells of affected individuals, it deposits most robustly in neurons.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Lipofuscin accumulation is concurrent with rapid and progressive neurodegeneration, particularly of thalamic and primary sensory cortical areas.
source: This accumulation is concurrent with rapid and progressive neurodegeneration, particularly of thalamic and primary sensory cortical areas (Bible et al., 2004; Kielar et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bible et al., 2004 and Kielar et al., 2007.

claim: NCLs are categorized into CLN1-14 based on the age of onset and the causative gene mutated.
source: The NCLs are categorized into CLN1-14 based on the age of onset and the causative gene mutated.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: NCLs are classified as lysosomal storage disorders (LSDs).
source: The products of CLN genes are lysosomal and endosomal proteins, therefore NCLs are also classified as lysosomal storage disorders (LSDs) (Bennett and Hofmann, 1999; Jalanko and Braulke, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bennett and Hofmann, 1999 and Jalanko and Braulke, 2009.

claim: CLN1 presents as early as 6 months of age with progressive psychomotor deterioration, seizure, and death at approximately 5 years of age.
source: The infantile form of disease, CLN1, presents as early as 6 months of age with progressive psychomotor deterioration, seizure, and death at approximately 5 years of age (Haltia, 2006; Jalanko and Braulke, 2009; Nita et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Haltia, 2006, Jalanko and Braulke, 2009, and Nita et al., 2016.

claim: CLN1 disease is caused by mutations in the gene CLN1, which encodes the enzyme palmitoyl-protein thioesterase 1 (PPT1).
source: CLN1 disease is caused by mutations in the gene CLN1, which encodes the enzyme palmitoyl-protein thioesterase 1 (PPT1)(Camp and Hofmann, 1993; Camp et al., 1994; Vesa et al., 1995; Jalanko and Braulke, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Camp and Hofmann, 1993, Camp et al., 1994, Vesa et al., 1995, and Jalanko and Braulke, 2009.

claim: PPT1 is a depalmitoylating enzyme responsible for the removal of palmitic acid from modified proteins.
source: PPT1 is a depalmitoylating enzyme responsible for the removal of palmitic acid from modified proteins (Camp and Hofmann, 1993; Lu and Hofmann, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Camp and Hofmann, 1993 and Lu and Hofmann, 2006.

claim: Protein palmitoylation is a crucial regulator of protein trafficking and function, particularly in neurons.
source: Protein palmitoylation, the addition of a 16-carbon fatty acid (palmitic acid) to cysteine residues, is a crucial regulator of protein trafficking and function, particularly in neurons (Hayashi et al., 2005; Hayashi et al., 2009; Fukata et al., 2006; Kang et al., 2008; Fukata and Fukata, 2010; Han et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hayashi et al., 2005, Hayashi et al., 2009, Fukata et al., 2006, Kang et al., 2008, Fukata and Fukata, 2010, and Han et al., 2015.

claim: Protein palmitoylation is mediated by palmitoyl acyltransferases (PATs) of the DHHC enzyme family.
source: This post-translational modification is mediated by palmitoyl acyltransferases (PATs) of the DHHC enzyme family (Fukata et al., 2006; Fukata and Fukata, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fukata et al., 2006 and Fukata and Fukata, 2010.

claim: Palmitoylation occurs via a reversible thioester bond (s-palmitoylation), permitting dynamic control over target protein interactions and function.
source: In contrast to other types of protein acylation, palmitoylation occurs via a reversible thioester bond (s-palmitoylation), permitting dynamic control over target protein interactions and function.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Palmitoylated proteins require depalmitoylation prior to lysosomal degradation.
source: Further, palmitoylated proteins require depalmitoylation prior to lysosomal degradation (Lu et al., 1996; Lu and Hofmann, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lu et al., 1996 and Lu and Hofmann, 2006.

claim: Protein palmitoylation and depalmitoylation contribute significantly to mechanisms underlying synaptic plasticity and endosomal-lysosomal trafficking of proteins.
source: Consequently, protein palmitoylation and depalmitoylation contribute significantly to mechanisms underlying synaptic plasticity and endosomal-lysosomal trafficking of proteins (Hayashi et al., 2005; Hayashi et al., 2009; Kang et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2009; Noritake et al., 2009; Fukata and Fukata, 2010; Mattison et al., 2012; Thomas et al., 2012; Thomas et al., 2013; Fukata et al., 2013; Han et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: PPT1 is a lysosomal depalmitoylating enzyme that localizes to the axonal and synaptic compartments.
source: Indeed, PPT1 is a lysosomal depalmitoylating enzyme that localizes to the axonal and synaptic compartments (Verkruyse and Hofmann, 1996; Ahtiainen et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Verkruyse and Hofmann, 1996, Ahtiainen et al., 2003, and Kim et al., 2008.

claim: Many synaptic proteins undergo palmitoylation, including PSD-95, all GluA subunits of AMPARs, and the GluN2A/2B subunits of NMDARs.
source: Many synaptic proteins undergo palmitoylation, including, but not limited to postsynaptic density protein 95 (PSD-95), all GluA subunits of AMPARs, and the GluN2A/2B subunits of NMDARs (Kang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kang et al., 2008.

claim: NMDARs are voltage-dependent, glutamate-gated ion channels consisting of two obligatory GluN1 subunits and two GluN2 subunits that undergo a developmental change.
source: N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) are voltage-dependent, glutamate-gated ion channels consisting of two obligatory GluN1 subunits and two GluN2 subunits that undergo a developmental change (Cull-Candy et al., 2001; van Zundert et al., 2004; Lau and Zukin, 2007; Paoletti et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cull-Candy et al., 2001, van Zundert et al., 2004, Lau and Zukin, 2007, and Paoletti et al., 2013.

claim: NMDARs play a crucial role in synaptic transmission, postsynaptic signal integration, synaptic plasticity, and have been implicated in various neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders.
source: NMDARs play a crucial role in synaptic transmission, postsynaptic signal integration, synaptic plasticity, and have been implicated in various neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders (Lau and Zukin, 2007; Lakhan et al., 2013; Paoletti et al., 2013; Yamamoto et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lau and Zukin, 2007, Lakhan et al., 2013, Paoletti et al., 2013, and Yamamoto et al., 2015.

claim: NMDAR subunit composition, receptor localization, and downstream signaling mechanism undergo developmental regulation.
source: NMDAR subunit composition, receptor localization, and downstream signaling mechanism undergo developmental regulation (Watanabe et al., 1992; Monyer et al., 1994; Sheng et al., 1994; Li et al., 1998; Stocca and Vicini, 1998; Tovar and Westbrook, 1999; Losi et al., 2003; van Zundert et al., 2004; Paoletti et al., 2013; Wyllie et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: GluN2B-containing NMDARs are expressed neonatally and display prolonged decay kinetics, which allows comparatively increased calcium influx thought to facilitate forms of synaptic plasticity critical for neurodevelopment.
source: Specifically, GluN2B-containing NMDARs are expressed neonatally and display prolonged decay kinetics, which allows comparatively increased calcium influx thought to facilitate forms of synaptic plasticity critical for neurodevelopment (Sobczyk et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2008; Evans et al., 2012; Shipton and Paulsen, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: GluN2B-containing receptors are supplanted at the synapse by diheteromeric GluN1/GluN2A NMDARs or triheteromeric (GluN1/GluN2A/GluN2B) receptors in response to experience-dependent neuronal activity.
source: These GluN2B-containing receptors are supplanted at the synapse by diheteromeric GluN1/GluN2A NMDARs or triheteromeric (GluN1/GluN2A/GluN2B) receptors in response to experience-dependent neuronal activity (Quinlan et al., 1999b; Quinlan et al., 1999a; Tovar and Westbrook, 1999; Philpot et al., 2001; Liu et al., 2004; Paoletti et al., 2013; Tovar et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The developmental switch of GluN2B- to GluN2A-containing NMDARs during brain maturation is mediated by the postsynaptic scaffolding receptors, SAP102 and PSD-95, respectively.
source: This developmental switch of GluN2B- to GluN2A-containing NMDARs during brain maturation is mediated by the postsynaptic scaffolding receptors, SAP102 and PSD-95, respectively; SAP102-GluN2B-NMDAR complexes are replaced by PSD-95-GluN2A-NMDAR complexes in response to developmental, experience-dependent activity (Sans et al., 2000; van Zundert et al., 2004; Elias et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sans et al., 2000, van Zundert et al., 2004, and Elias et al., 2008.

claim: PSD-95, GluN2B, and GluN2A all undergo palmitoylation.
source: While PSD-95, GluN2B, and GluN2A all undergo palmitoylation, how depalmitoylation regulates the turnover of these proteins, let alone during the GluN2B to GluN2A subunit switch, is unclear.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Lipofuscin accumulated in the Ppt1-/- visual cortex shortly after eye-opening at postnatal day (P) 14, a timing earlier than previously documented.
source: We found that lipofuscin accumulated in the Ppt1-/- visual cortex shortly after eye-opening at postnatal day (P) 14, a timing earlier than previously documented (Gupta et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gupta et al., 2001 and implies comparison to previous findings.

claim: The developmental NMDAR subunit switch from GluN2B to GluN2A is stagnated in Ppt1-/- mice.
source: We demonstrate that the developmental N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) subunit switch from GluN2B to GluN2A is stagnated in Ppt1-/- mice.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ppt1-/- neurons exhibit immature evoked NMDAR currents and dendritic spine morphology in vivo.
source: Correspondingly, Ppt1-/- neurons exhibit immature evoked NMDAR currents and dendritic spine morphology in vivo.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dissociated Ppt1-/- cultured neurons show extrasynaptic, diffuse calcium influxes and enhanced vulnerability to NMDA-induced excitotoxicity.
source: Further, dissociated Ppt1-/- cultured neurons show extrasynaptic, diffuse calcium influxes and enhanced vulnerability to NMDA-induced excitotoxicity, reflecting the predominance of GluN2B-containing receptors.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ppt1-/- neurons demonstrate hyperpalmitoylation of GluN2B as well as Fyn kinase, which regulates surface retention of GluN2B.
source: Remarkably, Ppt1-/- neurons demonstrate hyperpalmitoylation of GluN2B as well as Fyn kinase, which regulates surface retention of GluN2B.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PPT1 plays a critical role in postsynapse maturation by facilitating the GluN2 subunit switch and proteostasis of palmitoylated proteins.
source: Thus, PPT1 plays a critical role in postsynapse maturation by facilitating the GluN2 subunit switch and proteostasis of palmitoylated proteins.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and represents a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Autofluorescent lipopigments (ALs) are detectable first at P14 in Ppt1-/- visual cortex.
source: We found that ALs are detectable first at P14 in Ppt1-/- visual cortex, earlier than previously reported at 3 or 6 months (Figure 1A–C)(Gupta et al., 2001; Blom et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A-C and citations to Gupta et al., 2001 and Blom et al., 2013.

claim: ALs accumulated rapidly through the critical period and plateaued by adulthood (P60).
source: Further, ALs accumulated rapidly through the critical period (Berardi et al., 2000; Hensch, 2005; Maffei and Turrigiano, 2008) and plateaued by adulthood (P60) (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A-C and citations to Berardi et al., 2000, Hensch, 2005, and Maffei and Turrigiano, 2008.

claim: GluN2A levels in synaptosomes were significantly lower in Ppt1-/- than WT at P33, P42, and P60.
source: Although GluN2B levels were comparable between WT and Ppt1-/- at all ages, GluN2A levels in synaptosomes were significantly lower in Ppt1-/- than WT (Figure 2A). This decrease was present at time points during, and just following, the critical period in visual cortical development (P33, P42, and P60).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The GluN2A/GluN2B ratio showed a robust and persistent decrease in Ppt1-/- visual cortex.
source: When analyzed as a ratio of GluN2A/GluN2B, a robust and persistent decrease is observed in Ppt1-/- visual cortex (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: GluN1 levels were unchanged between WT and Ppt1-/- in synaptosomes.
source: GluN1 levels were unchanged between WT and Ppt1-/- in synaptosomes (Figure 2C), indicating the selective obstruction of GluN2A incorporation into NMDARs.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PSD-95 levels reduced at P33-P60 in Ppt1-/- visual cortex.
source: While SAP102 levels remained unchanged, PSD-95 levels reduced at P33-P60, the same developmental time points where GluN2A expression also decreased (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PPT1 expression in synaptosomes is low at P11 and P14 and increases with age, reaching peak levels between P33 and P60.
source: Indeed, PPT1 expression in synaptosomes is low at P11 and P14 and increases with age, reaching peak levels between P33 and P60 (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The fast component (Af/Af +As) of NMDAR-ESPC amplitudes decreased in Ppt1-/- mice as compared to WT.
source: The fast component (Af/Af +As) of NMDAR-ESPC amplitudes decreased in Ppt1-/- mice as compared to WT, while the slow component (As/Af +As) increased (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Ppt1-/- neurons showed a significant increase in weighted decay time τw as compared to WT.
source: Further, Ppt1-/- neurons showed a significant increase in weighted decay time τw as compared to WT (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The rise time (time to peak amplitude) of Ppt1-/- NMDAR-EPSCs was slightly but significantly longer than WT.
source: Remarkably, the rise time (time to peak amplitude) of Ppt1-/- NMDAR-EPSCs was slightly but significantly longer than WT (Figure 3D), suggesting that the response involves the receptors more distant from the presynaptic release site.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Ro 25–6981 treatment significantly decreased the τw of NMDAR-EPSCs from the baseline in both WT and Ppt1-/- cells at P42.
source: Ro 25–6981 treatment significantly decreased the τw of NMDAR-EPSCs from the baseline in both WT and Ppt1-/- cells at P42 (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: No significant effects were present between WT and Ppt1-/- genotypes after Ro 25–6981 treatment by two-way ANOVA.
source: To our surprise, no significant effects were present between the two genotypes after Ro 25–6981 treatment by two-way ANOVA, suggesting that NMDARs are inhibited to the same degree in WT and Ppt1-/- cortices.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Ppt1-/- spines were longer and less voluminous compared to WT at P33.
source: Quantification of spine length and spine volume demonstrated that Ppt1-/- spines were longer and less voluminous compared to WT (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: The volume of dendritic spine heads was reduced in Ppt1-/- neurons at P33.
source: Further, the volume of dendritic spine heads was reduced in Ppt1-/- neurons (Figure 4E, inset).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E inset.

claim: Dendritic spine density was significantly increased in Ppt1-/- neurons at P33.
source: Interestingly, dendritic spine density was significantly increased in Ppt1-/- neurons, signifying dysregulated synapse formation or refinement in the Ppt1-/- brain (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: GluN2A, PSD-95, and GluN2A/GluN2B ratio levels showed reductions in Ppt1-/- neurons compared to WT at DIV18.
source: Importantly, GluN2A, PSD-95, and GluN2A/GluN2B ratio levels showed reductions in Ppt1-/- neurons compared to WT at DIV18, indicating that the biochemical phenotype is recapitulated to an extent in vitro (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: The distribution of spine length in Ppt1-/- neurons at DIV15 significantly shifted toward longer protrusions as compared to WT cells.
source: The distribution of spine length in Ppt1-/- neurons at DIV15 significantly shifted toward longer protrusions as compared to WT cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The averaged spine length was robustly increased in Ppt1-/- neurons at DIV15.
source: The averaged spine length was also robustly increased in Ppt1-/- neurons (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Ppt1-/- neurons exhibit a significant reduction in the percentage of spines with volumes greater than ~0.2 μm3 at both DIV15 and DIV20.
source: Ppt1-/- neurons exhibit a significant reduction in the percentage of spines with volumes greater than ~0.2 μm3 at both DIV15 (Figure 6F) and DIV20 (Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6F and 6H.

claim: The averaged spine volume was reduced in Ppt1-/- neurons at both DIV15 and DIV20.
source: The averaged spine volume was also reduced in Ppt1-/- neurons at both DIV15 (Figure 6G) and DIV20 (Figure 6I).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6G and 6I.

claim: Ppt1-/- neurons showed an increase in the dendritic spine density at DIV15 and DIV20.
source: As observed in vivo, Ppt1-/- neurons showed an increase in the dendritic spine density at DIV15 (Figure 6J) and DIV20 (Figure 6K), again suggesting aberrant synapse formation, a failure of synaptic pruning, or both in Ppt1-/- neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6J and 6K.

claim: WT neurons exhibited primarily compartmentalized calcium signals that were restricted to individual spines.
source: While WT neurons exhibited primarily compartmentalized calcium signals that were restricted to individual spines (Figure 7A–C, left, see Video 1), Ppt1-/- neurons demonstrated diffuse calcium influxes that spread through the dendritic shaft (Figure 7A–C, right, see Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A-C and Video 1.

claim: Ppt1-/- neurons demonstrated diffuse calcium influxes that spread through the dendritic shaft.
source: While WT neurons exhibited primarily compartmentalized calcium signals that were restricted to individual spines (Figure 7A–C, left, see Video 1), Ppt1-/- neurons demonstrated diffuse calcium influxes that spread through the dendritic shaft (Figure 7A–C, right, see Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A-C and Video 2.

claim: There was a robust increase in both the AUC and the calcium diffusion distance in Ppt1-/- neurons compared to WT.
source: These analyses revealed a robust increase in both the AUC (Figure 7D) and the calcium diffusion distance (Figure 7E) in Ppt1-/- neurons compared to WT.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D and 7E.

claim: Calcium influxes are more synchronous (increased correlation coefficient) in Ppt1-/- neurons compared to WT.
source: Furthermore, performing correlation analysis of calcium events across time (see Materials and methods) within a given neuron demonstrates that calcium influxes are more synchronous (increased correlation coefficient) in Ppt1-/- neurons compared to WT (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Ro 25–6981 had virtually no effect on calcium signals recorded from WT cells.
source: Ro 25–6981 had virtually no effect on calcium signals recorded from WT cells (Figure 7G–I, see Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7G-I and Video 3.

claim: Ppt1-/- neurons treated with Ro 25–6981 showed a reduction in dendritic calcium influxes within shafts.
source: In contrast, Ppt1-/- neurons treated with Ro 25–6981 showed a reduction in dendritic calcium influxes within shafts, while few residual, compartmentalized transients persisted (Figure 7G–I, see Video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7G-I and Video 4.

claim: Both AUC and calcium diffusion distance were rescued to WT levels following Ro 25–6981 treatment of Ppt1-/- neurons.
source: Quantitatively, both AUC (Figure 7H) and calcium diffusion (Figure 7I) distance were rescued to WT levels following Ro 25–6981 treatment of Ppt1-/- neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7H and 7I.

claim: Ppt1-/- neurons were more vulnerable to NMDA insult, as exposure to 10 μM NMDA was sufficient to reduce cell viability significantly in Ppt1-/- neurons but not WT cells.
source: Importantly, Ppt1-/- neurons were more vulnerable to NMDA insult, as exposure to 10 μM NMDA was sufficient to reduce cell viability significantly in Ppt1-/- neurons but not WT cells (WT = 93 ± 4.1%; Ppt1-/- = 76 ± 3.5%; *p=0.046; Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: At 100 μM NMDA, WT neuron viability decreased by 35%, while Ppt1-/- neuron viability was reduced significantly further, by 58%.
source: Further, at 100 μM NMDA, WT neuron viability decreased by 35%, while Ppt1-/- neuron viability was reduced significantly further, by 58% (WT = 65 ± 1.8%; Ppt1-/- = 42 ± 4.5%; **p=0.0043; Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: 77% of cultured Ppt1-/- neurons accumulate ALs spontaneously at DIV18-20.
source: First, we found that 77% of cultured Ppt1-/- neurons accumulate ALs spontaneously at DIV18-20 (Figure 9A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9A and 9B.

claim: Treatment with the palmitoylation inhibitors, 2-bromopalmitate (2 BP, 1 μM, 7 day treatment) and cerulenin (1 μM, 7 day treatment) reduced the percentage of AL-positive neurons.
source: Treatment with the palmitoylation inhibitors, 2-bromopalmitate (2 BP, 1 μM, 7 day treatment) and cerulenin (1 μM, 7 day treatment) reduced the percentage of AL-positive neurons (Figure 9C) and the area occupied with ALs per neuron (Figure 9D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9C and 9D.

claim: The mean lysosomal size normalized in Ppt1-/- neurons when these cells were treated with 2 BP or cerulenin.
source: Further, the mean lysosomal size also normalized in Ppt1-/- neurons when these cells were treated with 2 BP or cerulenin (Figure 9E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: Pretreatment with both 2 BP and cerulenin improved cell viability of Ppt1-/- neurons to that of WT following excitotoxicity induction.
source: Notably, pretreatment with both 2 BP and cerulenin improved cell viability of Ppt1-/- neurons to that of WT following excitotoxicity induction, while the chronic low-dose treatment alone had no effect on neuronal viability (Figure 9F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9F.

claim: Treatment with both 2 BP and cerulenin decreased the AUCs of specified synapses compared to untreated Ppt1-/- cells, nearly to WT levels.
source: Notably, treatment with both 2 BP and cerulenin decreased the AUCs of specified synapses compared to untreated Ppt1-/- cells (see Video 7), nearly to WT levels (Figure 10A), indicating more compartmentalized calcium influx.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10A and Video 7.

claim: Calcium transient frequency was higher in Ppt1-/- cells than in WT but was lowest in Ppt1-/- neurons treated with 2 BP or cerulenin.
source: Further, calcium transient frequency was higher in Ppt1-/- cells than in WT but was lowest in Ppt1-/- neurons treated with 2 BP or cerulenin (Figure 10C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10C and 10D.

claim: The palmitoylation states of PSD-95 were comparable between Ppt1-/- and WT neurons.
source: Remarkably, the palmitoylation states of PSD-95 were comparable between Ppt1-/- and WT neurons (Figure 11C), suggesting that PSD-95 may not be a PPT1 substrate.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11C.

claim: 2 BP treatment decreased the relative palmitoylation level (ratio of palm/non-palm) of PSD-95 by nearly 50% in WT neurons.
source: Further, in line with previous data (El-Husseini et al., 2002; Fukata et al., 2013), 2 BP treatment decreased the relative palmitoylation level (ratio of palm/non-palm) of PSD-95 by nearly 50% in WT neurons (Figure 11C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11C and citations to El-Husseini et al., 2002 and Fukata et al., 2013.

claim: Total levels of Fyn were increased in Ppt1-/- neurons compared to WT.
source: Indeed, total levels of Fyn were increased in Ppt1-/- neurons compared to WT, and were significantly suppressed by 2 BP and cerulenin treatment in both WT and Ppt1-/- neurons (Figure 11E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11E.

claim: 2 BP and cerulenin treatments significantly reduced the ratio of palmitoylated/non-palmitoylated Fyn in WT and Ppt1-/- neurons.
source: 2 BP and cerulenin treatments also significantly reduced the ratio of palmitoylated/non-palmitoylated Fyn in WT and Ppt1-/- neurons (Figure 11F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11F.

claim: Total GluN2B levels were comparable between WT and Ppt1-/-, vehicle-treated neurons at DIV18.
source: First, total GluN2B levels were comparable between WT and Ppt1-/-, vehicle-treated neurons at DIV18 (Figure 11G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11G and 11H.

claim: Both 2 BP and cerulenin corrected the ratio of palmitoylated/non-palmitoylated GluN2B in Ppt1-/- neurons, with values approaching those of vehicle-treated WT cells.
source: Importantly, both 2 BP and cerulenin corrected the ratio of palmitoylated/non-palmitoylated GluN2B in Ppt1-/- neurons, with values approaching those of vehicle-treated WT cells (Figure 11I).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11I.

claim: Ppt1-/- neurons showed decreases in the band intensity of total GluN2A level as compared to WT.
source: As we found in our biochemical analyses of the cortical homogenates (Figures 2 and 5), Ppt1-/- neurons showed decreases in the band intensity of total GluN2A level as compared to WT (Figure 11J and K).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11J and 11K.

claim: The palmitoylation state (ratio of palm/non-palm) of GluN2A was unchanged between WT and Ppt1-/- at baseline.
source: The palmitoylation state (ratio of palm/non-palm) of GluN2A, however, was unchanged between WT and Ppt1-/- at baseline (Figure 11L), suggesting that PPT1 is not directly involved in the palmitoylation state of GluN2A.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11L.

claim: 2 BP treatment in Ppt1-/- neurons robustly increased both the total level and palmitoylation state of GluN2A.
source: In contrast, 2 BP treatment in Ppt1-/- neurons robustly increased both the total level and palmitoylation state of GluN2A, resulting in the nearly equal representation of two distinct GluN2A palmitoylated species (Figure 11K and L).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11K and 11L.

claim: Cerulenin treatment of Ppt1-/- cells increased the total GluN2A protein level.
source: In contrast, cerulenin treatment of Ppt1-/- cells increased the total GluN2A protein level (Figure 11K and L), albeit not nearly as robustly as 2 BP.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11K and 11L.

claim: The rodent visual cortex undergoes timed, experience-dependent plasticity.
source: The rodent visual cortex undergoes timed, experience-dependent plasticity, which has been well-characterized at the systemic, cellular, and molecular levels (Bear et al., 1990; Gordon and Stryker, 1996; Hensch et al., 1998; Quinlan et al., 1999a; Fagiolini and Hensch, 2000; Mataga et al., 2001; Mataga et al., 2004; Philpot et al., 2001; Desai et al., 2002; Yoshii et al., 2003; Hensch, 2005; Cooke and Bear, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: In mice, P11 and P14 are prior to and just after eye opening (EO), respectively.
